problem: Both output-characteristic curves are drawn as perfectly horizontal lines all the way down to V_CE = 0. A real BJT has I_C falling steeply below V_CE ≈ 0.3 V (saturation), and Section 3 of this same chapter says the real curves tilt upward with V_CE. A student may read the plot as meaning r_o is infinite and that the collector current stays at 4.71 mA even at V_CE = 0.
fix: Draw the I_B curves only for V_CE ≥ 0.3 V, with a slight upward tilt (Early effect), and drop them steeply toward zero below 0.3 V; or add a note that the curves are idealized and flat only as a first approximation.

problem: The curve labelled I_B = 24 µA is placed at 2.36 mA. With β = 100 (the value used in the worked example on the same page) the current should be 2.4 mA; 2.36 mA is exactly half of 4.71 mA, so the label and the ordinate disagree by about 2 %.
fix: Label the lower curve I_B ≈ 23.5 µA, or move it to 2.4 mA.

problem: "Temperature and transistor gain drift, so the bias network must hold the point nearly fixed." The verb "drift" is buried at the end and a second-language reader can read the sentence as a list of two nouns with no predicate.
fix: Temperature and transistor gain both drift, so the bias network must hold the Q-point nearly fixed.

problem: "The Early voltage matters more as supply voltages fall, because r_o drops and gain falls with it." Lowering the supply does not by itself lower r_o: r_o ≈ V_A/I_C depends on the bias current, and the (V_A + V_CE) correction is tiny when V_CE is a fraction of a volt. The real reason the Early effect hurts at low supply is the reduced voltage headroom, not a drop in r_o.
fix: Say that the Early effect matters more as supply voltages fall because the available V_CE swing shrinks, so a tilted characteristic eats into the usable output range.
